strengths: Principled, biologically grounded architecture: The proposed Uni-NTFM thoughtfully addresses the physical nature of EEG signals by decoupling time-domain transients and spectral rhythms via HFPM and DCM, rather than naively treating EEG as 1D text or 2D image patches.

Unification across heterogeneous sensor montages: The hierarchical Topological Embedding (combining region, intra-region, and absolute spatial positions) provides a robust solution to montage mismatch, as validated by strong cross-montage transfer and missing-electrode stress tests.

Impressive scale and efficiency: Pre-training on 28,000 hours of multi-source EEG data and scaling up to 1.9B parameters using a sparse MoE Transformer represents one of the largest foundation models in the EEG / neural decoding domain, with sparse routing keeping inference FLOPs competitive.

Comprehensive downstream evaluation and analysis: The model is rigorously tested across 9 diverse downstream benchmarks under both linear probing and fine-tuning. The paper also includes extensive scaling-law studies (varying both model size and pre-training data volume), MoE routing visualizations, and detailed component ablations.
weaknesses: Holistic per-channel tokenization: By collapsing the entire temporal window into a single token per electrode, the spatial MoE Transformer primarily models inter-channel relationships, which may limit the model's capacity to resolve fine-grained temporal event sequencing or sub-second dynamic interactions across channels.

Application of 1D RoPE to spatial electrode sequences: Applying 1D Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) relies on an arbitrary sequential ordering of electrodes on a continuous 2D/3D cortical surface, which could introduce artificial sequential biases despite the topological embeddings.

Performance saturation at large parameter scales: The scaling experiments (Appendix H) show that downstream gains plateau or slightly regress beyond ~800M parameters under the 10,000-hour setting, indicating that the 1.9B parameter capacity might not be fully unlocked without even larger corpora.

Minor presentation omissions: The code repository URLs in the Abstract and Reproducibility section are left empty ('available at'), along with minor typos in the text (e.g., 'processd' in Section 2.1, 'explaination' in Section 2.2.3, 'transfor' in Section 4, and 'Bssides' in Appendix L).

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The proposed Uni-NTFM is evaluated across nine diverse downstream EEG benchmarks covering clinical diagnosis, emotion recognition, cognitive workload, sleep staging, and motor imagery under both linear probing and fine-tuning protocols.

Principled, domain-tailored architectural design: Rather than naively adapting vision/language Transformers, the model incorporates biologically inspired mechanisms—specifically a dual-stream time/frequency projection (HFPM), cross-attention fusion (DCM), and a hierarchical topological embedding (TE) to accommodate heterogeneous electrode montages.

Effective use of Sparse MoE: The paper scales the EEG foundation model up to 1.9B parameters while constraining active inference FLOPs and latency, decoupling model capacity from computational cost, and provides detailed visualizations of expert routing across network depth and anatomical regions.

Extensive ablations and robustness analyses: The submission includes thorough analyses of individual components (HFPM, DCM, TE, MoE), model/data scaling laws, robustness against missing channels, cross-montage zero-shot transfer, and label efficiency.
weaknesses: Unfinished placeholders and minor proofreading issues: In both the Abstract (page 1) and Reproducibility statement (page 11), the sentence ends abruptly with 'Our code is available at ' without providing an anonymous repository URL. Several typos exist in the text (e.g., 'processd' on p. 3, 'Bssides' on p. 29, 'similer' and 'domenstrate' on p. 28).

Inconsistency in dataset specifications: In Table 7, the SEED dataset is listed as having a '5-class' label, whereas in Table 1 and Section 3.3 it is evaluated and referred to as a 3-class task (which is the standard SEED specification, distinguishing it from SEED-V).

Limited discussion on temporal tokenization and variable signal lengths: Treating the entire channel time series (T=1600 samples, corresponding to 8s at 200 Hz) as a single holistic patch simplifies spatial cross-attention across electrodes, but leaves open questions about how the architecture handles longer or varying-duration EEG recordings common in continuous clinical monitoring.

strengths: Large-scale pre-training effort: The paper aggregates approximately 28,000 hours of multi-source EEG data across diverse clinical, cognitive, and BCI paradigms, scaling the model capacity up to 1.9 billion parameters using a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture.

Comprehensive downstream evaluation: The framework is benchmarked across nine distinct downstream tasks spanning abnormal EEG detection, event classification, emotion recognition, motor imagery, and sleep staging under both linear probing and full fine-tuning protocols.

Extensive ablation and diagnostic experiments: The appendix provides extensive supplementary analyses, including MoE routing and expert-region affinity visualizations, cross-montage transfer, resilience to missing channels, and empirical scaling analyses across data and parameter sizes.
weaknesses: Severe risk of pre-training data contamination / leakage: The pre-training corpus incorporates the massive Temple University Hospital EEG corpus (TUEG, 27,100 hours), while downstream evaluation heavily relies on TUAB, TUEV, and TUSL—which are subsets and specific re-annotations of the TUEG archive. The paper does not describe any subject-level or recording-level deduplication to ensure that downstream test subjects were strictly excluded from the pre-training set.

Questionable spatial-temporal tokenization and position encoding: By collapsing the entire time window ($T = 1600$) of each electrode into a single feature vector, the Transformer operates solely over electrode tokens, effectively discarding fine-grained temporal-dynamic interactions across time. Furthermore, applying 1D Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) across the flattened electrode index sequence imposes an arbitrary 1D ordering on non-sequential 2D/3D scalp sensor coordinates.

Ambiguity and collapse risk in the reconstruction objective: In Equations 14–16, the temporal reconstruction loss targets $h_{i,R} = \Phi_R(x_i)$, an embedding generated by a 'Standard Projection Encoder', rather than the raw signal itself or a fixed tokenizer. The paper lacks technical details on how $\Phi_R$ is trained or constrained to prevent trivial representation collapse.

Disproportionate model scale and poor parameter efficiency: Despite scaling to 1.9 billion total parameters (307M active parameters), Uni-NTFM yields marginal or no improvements compared to significantly smaller existing foundation models. For example, LaBraM-Base (5.8M parameters) achieves a higher AUROC on TUAB (90.22% vs. 89.64%), and CSBrain outperforms Uni-NTFMlarge on TUSL (85.71% vs. 78.44% Balanced Accuracy).

Missing links and presentation oversights: Unfilled placeholder text exists in the abstract ('Our code is available at') and the Reproducibility section ('released under an open-source license at'), along with several typographical errors throughout the text.

strengths: Substantial pre-training scale: Pre-trained on over 28,000 hours of diverse EEG data with model configurations scaling up to 1.9B parameters, representing one of the largest efforts in EEG representation learning to date.

Comprehensive downstream evaluation: Evaluated across nine diverse EEG benchmark tasks covering clinical diagnosis (TUAB, TUEV, TUSL), emotion recognition (SEED), sleep staging (HMC), and brain-computer interfaces (BCIC-IV-2a), under both linear probing and fine-tuning settings.

Well-motivated architecture: The integration of multi-domain feature decoupling (time, frequency, raw lossless reference), cross-attention fusion, and a dual-domain self-supervised reconstruction objective aligns well with the known spectral and temporal properties of EEG signals.

Thorough ablations and scaling experiments: Detailed component-wise ablations validate the contributions of HFPM, DCM, TE, and MoE. The paper also includes empirical scaling law studies across both parameter count (10M to 1B) and pre-training data volume.
weaknesses: Overstated comparative performance: The text states that Uni-NTFM comprehensively outperforms all baseline models across all nine tasks. However, in Table 3, CSBrain outperforms Uni-NTFM on several metrics (e.g., TUSL Balanced Accuracy of 0.8571 vs. 0.7844; HMC Balanced Accuracy of 0.7345 vs. 0.7311). The claims regarding consistent superiority across all benchmarks should be toned down.

Ambiguity in topological coordinate mapping across differing montages: In Section 2.3 and Algorithm 2, equations (32) and (33) compute region and intra-region indices using integer arithmetic on a flattened index j (i.e., floor(j/E) and j mod E). It is unclear how this simple modular indexing robustly maps differing electrode montages (e.g., 19 channels in CAUEEG vs. 64 channels in REEG-BACA) onto canonical neuroanatomical positions without a predefined canonical coordinate or lookup table.
Missing details on MoE configuration: The Top-k gating hyperparameter (e.g., Top-1 vs. Top-2) and the routing capacity factor are not explicitly stated in the main paper or the parameter tables.

Minor formatting errors: Table 1 contains an unresolved reference (`EEGNet (?)`), and minor typos exist in the text (e.g., 'Topological Embeddin', 'eterogeneous Feature Projection Module', 'transfor into').

strengths: Scale and ambition: Uni-NTFM scales up to 1.9B parameters and is pretrained on over 28,000 hours of diverse EEG recordings across 9 public datasets, representing one of the largest foundation models in the EEG domain to date.

Domain-motivated architecture: Decoupling the input into time-domain local waveforms, frequency-domain spectral band powers, and raw references via HFPM and cross-attending them via DCM is well-aligned with the physical characteristics of EEG signals.
Sparsely-activated MoE design: Replacing dense Transformer FFN layers with a top-k MoE helps scale parameter capacity while maintaining manageable computation during training.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper conducts evaluations across 9 diverse downstream tasks spanning clinical diagnosis, event classification, BCI motor imagery, sleep scoring, and cognitive workload under both linear probing and fine-tuning regimes, complemented by systematic scaling law analyses (varying model size from 10M to 1B and pretraining data from 1.5k to 12k hours).
weaknesses: Unclear topological embedding implementation across variable montages: In Section 2.3 and Algorithm 2, equations (32)–(33) compute region and intra-region indices using integer division and modulo operations based on sequence index ($I_{region}^{(j)} = \lfloor j/E \rfloor$, $I_{intra}^{(j)} = j \pmod E$). Downstream datasets vary widely in channel counts (e.g., 4 channels in HMC, 19 in CAUEEG, 22 in BCIC-IV-2a, 62 in SEED). It is unclear how arbitrary electrode channels from different montages are mapped onto the predefined $(R, E)$ template so that identical indices correspond to the same anatomical coordinates.

Overstated comparative claims against state-of-the-art baselines: The abstract and introduction claim that Uni-NTFM significantly outperforms all foundation models across nine tasks. However, Table 3 shows that CSBrain substantially outperforms Uni-NTFM on TUSL (CSBrain achieves 0.8571 Balanced Acc vs. Uni-NTFM-large's 0.7844; Kappa 0.7828 vs. 0.6853). Additionally, in Table 1 on TUAB, LaBraM-Base outperforms Uni-NTFM-large in AUROC (0.9022 vs. 0.8964). These discrepancies should be transparently discussed rather than claiming universal SOTA.

Lack of analysis for claimed MoE functional specialization: A central conceptual justification for the MoE architecture is routing functionally distinct EEG patterns (e.g., specific rhythmic frequencies, artifacts, pathological waveforms) to specialized subnetworks. However, no routing visualizations, expert gate statistics, or qualitative analyses are provided to verify whether functional specialization actually emerges.

Handling of variable temporal lengths: Treating the entire channel recording as a holistic patch requires clarifying how the model handles arbitrary recording durations across datasets beyond the fixed sequence length of $T=1600$ (8 seconds at 200 Hz). The windowing/aggregation strategy during inference should be clearly stated.

Writing and proofreading errors: Several typographical errors remain in key sections, such as 'eterogeneous' (Section 2.2), 'Topological Embeddin' (Section 2.3), and 'transfor into the scalable MoE' (Section 4).

strengths: Ambitious Pre-training Scale: The paper attempts an extensive pre-training effort in the EEG domain, scaling up to 1.9B parameters and utilizing over 28,000 hours of multi-source EEG data across diverse clinical and BCI domains.

Comprehensive Benchmark Suite: The empirical evaluation spans nine distinct EEG datasets covering multiple clinical and non-clinical tasks (e.g., TUAB, TUEV, SEED, TDBrain, ADFTD, BCIC-IV-2a, Workload, HMC, TUSL) across both linear probing and fine-tuning paradigms.
Inclusion of Scaling Analysis: The paper provides empirical explorations of both parameter scaling (from 10M to 1B) and dataset size scaling (from 1,500 to 12,000 hours).
weaknesses: Severe Discrepancies and Inconsistencies Across Experimental Results: There is a striking numerical inconsistency between the main results (Tables 1-3) and the scaling analysis tables (Tables 12-13). For example, in Table 1, Uni-NTFM_tiny (57M) achieves a Balanced Accuracy of 0.7136 (linear probing) and 0.7649 (fine-tuned) on TUAB. However, in Table 12, the ~50M model achieves only 0.6179 (linear probing) and 0.6492 (fine-tuned). Even when scaling data up to 12,000 hours for the 57M model in Table 13, the fine-tuned Balanced Accuracy is only 0.6567 with clear signs of diminishing returns, making the leap to 0.7649 at 28,000 hours mathematically implausible and indicative of differing evaluation protocols, data leakage, or unverified figures.

Questionable Architectural Design and Temporal Collapse: In Section 2.2, the authors state that rather than tokenizing temporal patches, they treat the entire time series (e.g., T=1600 time steps) of an electrode as a single holistic patch and collapse it into a single D-dimensional vector. Collapsing an entire multi-second EEG recording per channel into one vector severely constrains temporal resolution. Furthermore, the Dual-domain Cross-attention Module (DCM) performs cross-attention across electrodes prior to injecting spatial coordinates, conflating cross-electrode functional connectivity with cross-domain (temporal vs. spectral) feature interaction.

Superficial Topological Modeling: While presented as a neuroscience-grounded 'hierarchical Topological Embedding mechanism', Equations 32-33 and Algorithm 2 reveal that region and intra-region indices are computed simply by integer division and modulo operations over electrode indices (i.e., floor(j / E) and j mod E). This is an arbitrary linear indexing heuristic rather than an anatomical coordinate system, failing to explain how heterogeneous electrode montages across datasets (ranging from 4 channels in HMC to 64 channels in BioSemi) are genuinely unified or mapped in physical space.

Unsubstantiated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Specialization Claims: The authors assert that replacing FFNs with MoE enables specialized routing for specific neural rhythms, artifacts, and pathological waveforms. However, no router analysis, expert utilization statistics, or qualitative validation of expert specialization are provided to substantiate this claim.

Potential Target Collapse in Dual-Domain Reconstruction: In the self-supervised objective (Eq. 15), the temporal reconstruction loss reconstructs the output of Phi_R(x_i), where Phi_R is an encoder projection. If Phi_R is trained simultaneously without a stop-gradient or exponential moving average (EMA) mechanism, the reconstruction objective risks representation collapse.

Draft Incompleteness and Poor Polishing: The manuscript contains notable formatting oversights, typos, and unfinished sections: empty URLs in the Abstract, Introduction, and Reproducibility sections ('Our code is available at '); broken citations ('EEGNet (?)' in Table 1); conflicting challenge counts ('three core architectural challenges' followed by four numbered points in Section 1); and numerous typographical errors ('eterogeneous', 'Embeddin', 'transfor', 'explaination').
